title: Faucet Repair Fundamentals: Handle Removal, Washer/Seat Inspection, and Seal Repair
summary: This Old House presents a hands-on guide to repairing a leaking faucet, starting with how to remove the handle (including hidden screws and the use of a handle puller for stubborn fittings), then distinguishing between modern cartridge-based faucets and traditional stem-and-washer designs. The video proceeds to inspect the bottom washer and the associated screw, highlighting wear and the risk of stripping a screw head. For older valves, it demonstrates removing and inspecting the valve seat, and discusses options to restore a tight seal—ranging from replacing washers and ends to using a seat wrench, grinding or reaming the seat, or replacing the seat itself—and emphasizes that a proper seal hinges on mating flat surfaces between the washer and the seat.
topics: end of stem wear and retainer ring

sections.description: Introductory primer on how to remove a faucet handle, including locating the small screw under a button cover, how to push and counterclockwise turn, and using a handle puller when mineral buildup fuses the handle. The segment also explains the difference between modern cartridge faucets and older stem-based configurations, including how water flow is controlled and where to expect a cartridge versus a stubby stem.

sections.description: Discussion moves into older, traditional faucets with a stem unit, where the bottom washer and its seat are critical. It covers identifying the type of faucet, recognizing that the bottom washer can be worn, and that screws seated in water over years are prone to stripping without proper tool contact. The segment emphasizes careful screwdriver technique to avoid head stripping and the consequences of a stripped screw.

sections.description: The final section covers reviving a leaking traditional faucet by addressing the end of the stem, including breaking off the worn end, grinding it to accommodate a retainer ring, and installing a new end. It then shows how to extract the seat with a seat wrench, evaluate for pitting or cracks, and choose among seating options (new seat, grinding with emery cloth, or seat reaming). The overarching principle is achieving a tight seal between the washer and the seat to stop leaks.
